lectures.title: Arrays and Linked Lists
lectures.summary: Compared arrays and linked lists; amortized cost of dynamic array resizing.

lectures.title: Stacks and Queues
lectures.summary: Stack/queue operations; implementing a queue with two stacks.

lectures.title: Binary Heaps
lectures.summary: Binary heaps as complete binary trees stored in arrays. Insertion, extract-min, and building a heap in O(n).

topics.title: Heap property and array layout
topics.summary: Parent is smaller than children (min-heap); children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.

topics.title: Insertion (bubble up)
topics.summary: Insert at the end, then swap with the parent while smaller. O(log n).
topics.deep_note: Worked example: inserting 1 into [2,5,3] moves 1 to the root in two swaps.

topics.title: Extract-min (bubble down)
topics.summary: Move the last element to the root, then swap with the smaller child. O(log n).
topics.deep_note: Always swap with the smaller child to keep the heap property.

topics.title: Heapify in O(n)
topics.summary: Bottom-up heapify costs O(n), not O(n log n).
topics.deep_note: Most nodes are near the leaves, so most sift-downs are short.

lectures.title: Heapsort and Priority Queues
lectures.summary: Heapsort using a heap; priority queues; comparison of heapsort with quicksort.

topics.title: Heapsort
topics.summary: Build a heap, then extract repeatedly. O(n log n) worst case, in place.

topics.title: Priority queues
topics.summary: Heaps implement priority queues; used in scheduling and Dijkstra.

topics.title: Heapsort vs quicksort
topics.summary: Quicksort is usually faster in practice (cache-friendly) but worst case O(n^2); heapsort guarantees O(n log n).
topics.deep_note:
## Heapsort vs quicksort
The professor compared the two by average speed and guarantees: quicksort wins on average, heapsort wins on guarantees ⟦s000412-s000425⟧.

## Why quicksort is faster in practice
Quicksort scans memory sequentially, which is cache-friendly ⟦s000426-s000431⟧.

lectures.title: Binary Search Trees
lectures.summary: BST insert and search; deletion with 0, 1, or 2 children (replace with successor).

lectures.title: AVL Trees
lectures.summary: AVL trees keep heights balanced. The professor defines the balance factor as height(right) − height(left), the opposite of most textbooks. Four rotation cases.

topics.title: AVL definition
topics.summary: Heights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1.

topics.title: Balance factor convention
topics.summary: BF = height(right) − height(left). Left-heavy is negative. The test uses this convention.
topics.deep_note:
## Balance factor
BF = height(right) − height(left) ⟦s000233-s000240⟧. Standard textbooks use left − right, so signs are flipped. The professor said the test uses this convention ⟦s000241-s000243⟧.

topics.title: Single rotations (LL, RR)
topics.summary: LL: right rotation once. RR: left rotation once.

topics.title: Double rotations (LR, RL)
topics.summary: LR: rotate the child left, then the node right. RL is the mirror.

transcripts.C1/L4/s412-425: So which one should you use? Honestly, on average quicksort wins, it's just faster on real machines. But heapsort wins on guarantees. If someone hands you adversarial input, heapsort still gives you n log n. I like to say: quicksort is the sprinter, heapsort is the one that always finishes the marathon.
transcripts.C1/L4/s426-431: Part of why quicksort is fast is the cache. It walks through the array in order, so the memory it needs is usually already there.
transcripts.C1/L6/s233-240: Now, I'm going to define the balance factor as the height of the right subtree minus the height of the left. I know your textbook does it the other way around. I just find right minus left easier to draw.
transcripts.C1/L6/s241-243: And yes, on the exam I will use my convention, so please don't flip the signs.
transcripts.C4/L2/s518-526: Here's a trick I really like. Before you eliminate, swap rows so the entry with the largest absolute value becomes the pivot. It's called partial pivoting. On paper it saves you from ugly fractions, and on a computer it keeps rounding errors small.
transcripts.C4/L5/s610-618: Let me tell you a story. In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge started twisting in the wind until it collapsed. People often say it was resonance, which is really an eigenvalue story: the wind kept feeding energy into one mode of the bridge.
transcripts.C5/L4/s801-806: Quick aside, since we're talking about sensing tiny signals: last year's Nobel Prize in Physics went to work showing quantum tunneling in an electrical circuit you can hold in your hand. That's the physics behind superconducting qubits. Look it up, it's a great story.

recent_conversation: クイックソートとの違いは?
マージソートは統治(merge)が仕事をし、クイックソートはpivotでの分割が仕事をする。平均O(n log n)だが、クイックソートはpivotの選び方が悪いと最悪O(n²)。
pivotの選び方って重要なんだね
すごく重要。ランダムに選ぶか、中央値に近い値を選ぶ工夫で最悪ケースを避けやすくなる。
